gv_border_walker.text: {greeting} I walk out from Derry most Sundays. There used to be a checkpoint on this road, years ago. Now the only way you'd know you've crossed is the speed signs going metric.
Miles behind you, kilometres in front. My car does the sums. My legs refuse to.

else.text: Is that a cake for Áine in Donegal Town? Tell her the walker from Derry says happy birthday. Sure the whole road knows Áine.
Thirty-odd years ago there'd have been soldiers and a checkpoint here, and half the wee country roads blocked off.
The border runs about 500 kilometres, through farms, rivers and the odd front room. Thousands cross it every day for work and school.
Since Brexit it's the only land border between the UK and the EU. Everybody agreed on one thing: no checkpoints back. Getting there was the hard bit.
Noted in the Gazetteer, under How these isles work.

gv_eagle_watcher.text: Shh. There. No. That was a raven. Ravens tumble about for fun; a golden eagle just hangs there like it owns the sky. Which it does.
They were gone from Ireland for nearly a hundred years. The chicks for Glenveagh came over from Scotland from 2000 on, and now there are pairs nesting in the hills again.
Seven years old before they're properly grown up and breeding, you know. Teenagers with talons. I've a lot of sympathy.

gv_deer.text: A red deer lifts its head from the heather, chews thoughtfully, and decides you are not worth stopping lunch for.
In the autumn rut the stags roar across Glenveagh day and night. Right now it is just chewing, which is quieter.

gv_fiddler.text: I'm practising for a céilí. The castle gardens have the best acoustics in Donegal, if you don't count the midges, and I don't, because they count me.
This one's a highland. Donegal has its own highlands, a kind of tune, nothing to do with Scotland. Well. A bit to do with Scotland. Don't tell anyone.

gv_gardener.text: The gardens have plants from all over the world, sheltered by the trees and the hills. Rhododendrons, tree ferns, palms. Palms! In Donegal!
The Gulf Stream does half the work. I do the other half, and the slugs do their best to undo both.

gv_glen_poet.text: They call it the Poisoned Glen, but look at it. Granite walls, a stream, a ruined church. If this is poison, pour me a pint of it.
One story says Balor of the Evil Eye was killed hereabouts, and the poison of his eye split the rocks. The other says a mapmaker spelt 'heavenly' wrong. I prefer the mapmaker. He's more relatable.

then.text: Back again? The crotal grows slowly, love. I'm not scraping the mountain bald for one bolt of tweed.

else.text: Úna sent you for crotal? Good woman. This is it, the grey crusty lichen on the boulders. Boil it up with wool and you get the rust and brown of a proper Donegal tweed.
It grows about as fast as a glacier, so you only ever take a little, from a lot of stones. There.
Now you want the brighter colours. Nóra the weaver over in Gaoth Dobhair has heather and whin in her pots. Over the mountain, west.
{greeting} I'm picking crotal, the lichen off the rocks. The weavers dye wool with it. Smells like a wet dog when it's boiling, and the colour is worth every sniff.
Harris tweed in Scotland used it too. They call it crottle. We call it crotal. We have both been arguing about the spelling for two hundred years.

then.text: There they are, the conqueror of Errigal. Your legs will tell you about it tomorrow, at length.
You raced Ciarán at the summit, and won? He'll be mortified. He trains on that ridge in the dark.
Here, this is for you. A chip of the mountain itself. Quartzite, pink as the sunset, and twice as stubborn.
Seven hundred and fifty-one metres. Highest in Donegal. You'll be telling people that for years.
The path goes all the way round the mountain and up the east side. Keep to it; the scree will have your ankles. There's a fell runner at the top who'll want a race.

else.text: {greeting} That's Errigal, An Earagail, the highest mountain in the county. Quartzite all the way up, and it turns pink at sunset like it's embarrassed about something.
Fancy climbing it? It's a fair old walk.

then.text: Good on you. Follow the path round and up. At the top, find Ciarán the fell runner. He goes up and down it before his breakfast and he'll want a race. Come back and tell me how you got on.

else.text: It'll be there tomorrow. It's been there a few hundred million years.

gv_summit.text: You made it up! Isn't it something? Tory out on the sea, the Derryveagh Mountains all round, and the whole of Donegal under your boots.

then.text: I'm still getting my breath back after our race. And I do this every morning. Mortifying.

else.text: I run up here every morning. Fancy a race back down? Well. A battle. Racing down scree is how people end up on the news.

then.text: Go on and tell the guide at the bottom. He'll never believe it.
